source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Patterns Related to Yesterday: Breakouts, Breakout Pullbacks, and Failed Breakouts

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode, sides field says mirrored/same. Helpers: isFirstBarOfSession(n) as in V17-01; priorSessionHigh/priorSessionLow/priorSessionClose = the prior day's session high/low/close; ema = XAverage(close, emaLength); bullTrendBar(n)/bearTrendBar(n) = body-fraction test.

candidates.name: GapProxyByFirstBarVsEma
candidates.quote: If the first bar is entirely above the moving average, think of the open as a gap up. If the first bar is entirely below the moving average, assume that the market is gapping down.
candidates.description: Context filter classifying the open as a bullish (bearish) gap day when the first bar of the session sits entirely above (below) the EMA, used when the actual gap versus yesterday's close is ambiguous.

complexity.reason: session-boundary primitive plus an EMA comparison

notes: This is a stated proxy for an actual open-vs-yesterday's-close gap test, which is simpler and mechanizable directly on daily bars (see GapUpOnOpen-style rules mined from chapter 20).

candidates.name: OpeningRangeBreakoutTrendDay
candidates.quote: When the first 5 to 10 bars form a sideways range, many institutions enter on the breakout of the range, and this breakout often leads to a trend day.
candidates.description: The classic opening-range breakout: track the high/low of the first N bars of the session; once that window closes, enter long (short) on a break above (below) that range.
candidates.pseudocode: ctx.BarsIntoSession(0) > openingRangeBars && close[0] > highest(high, openingRangeBars, ctx.SessionStartBar(0))
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick above (long) / below (short) the opening range extreme

complexity.reason: needs a session-start marker to fix the opening-range window, then a highest/lowest over a bounded window; no pivot detection required

notes: Brooks gives a range of 5 to 10 bars; 8 used as a midpoint default.

candidates.name: FailedBreakoutReversalEntry
candidates.quote: If that bear breakout has follow-through for a few bars and then there is a strong bull reversal, this could set up a failed breakout and a possible low of the day.
candidates.description: After a breakout below a swing low (e.g. yesterday's low) with several bars of follow-through, a strong bull trend/reversal bar signals a failed breakout: enter long beyond that reversal bar.
candidates.pseudocode: close[followThroughBars] < swingLowBeforeBreakout && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && low[0] < lowest(low, followThroughBars)
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the reversal bar's high (long) / low (short)

complexity.reason: needs identification of the breakout level (a prior swing low/high or yesterday's extreme) and confirmation that price traveled beyond it before the reversal bar

notes: The 'swing low before breakout' term is intentionally left abstract; this composes with a swing-pivot primitive from other chapters (e.g. yesterday's session low, or a swing-detection primitive).

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackAfterFailedBreakoutFailure
candidates.quote: If the rally lasts only a bar or two and then there is another strong bear trend bar, the failed breakout might be failing. If so, shorting below that bear bar is a breakout pullback entry.
candidates.description: A failed-breakout reversal (V18-03) itself fails within a bar or two — a new strong trend bar reappears in the original breakout direction — re-entering in the original breakout direction beyond that bar (a breakout pullback / resumption trade).
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond this bar's low (short) / high (long)

complexity.reason: requires remembering that a failed-breakout reversal (itself a hard pattern) occurred within the last N bars and testing that the market has resumed in the breakout direction

notes: This is the book's two-stage failure logic: breakout -> failed breakout (reversal) -> failure of the failed breakout (resumption). Each stage is its own candidate; this one composes on top of V18-03.

candidates.name: TwiceFailedBreakoutExpectReversal
candidates.quote: The bar 7 double top... was the second failed attempt to break out above yesterday's high, and when the market tries to do something twice and fails, it usually tries to go in the opposite direction.
candidates.description: Context filter: after the market has attempted and failed to break a level (e.g. yesterday's high) twice within the session, expect the market to reverse in the opposite direction, favoring reversal entries over continuation.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter favoring reversal setups over continuation)

complexity.reason: requires tracking discrete 'attempts' at a level (touches followed by failure to close beyond it) across the session, not a single window statistic

notes: Brooks applies this specifically to failed breakouts of yesterday's high/low in this chapter, but states it as a general principle.

candidates.name: ReversalOffYesterdayCloseTest
candidates.quote: Bar 1 was a sharp pullback to test yesterday's strong close, and it quickly reversed up, creating a buy entry at one tick above the high of the bar 1 pullback.
candidates.description: Early in the session, price pulls back to touch (or come within a tick range of) yesterday's close and reverses with a bull bar: enter long beyond that reversal bar's high.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] <= priorSessionClose + touchTicks * tick && close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0])
candidates.book_order_type: stop one tick beyond the pullback bar's high (long) / low (short)

complexity.reason: a fixed reference price (yesterday's close) compared against the current bar's low/high plus a single-bar trend-bar test

notes: 'Test' is read as the bar's low (long case) coming within touchTicks of yesterday's close, not necessarily piercing it.

rejected.quote: Bar 8 was a signal bar for a breakout pullback long, following the breakout above the bar 6 top of the opening range... It was also a setup for a long based on the failed double top bear flag where bar 6 was the first top.
rejected.reason: one-off discretionary chart narration naming specific bar numbers on a specific historical chart; the general breakout-pullback and failed-breakout patterns it illustrates are captured as V18-02..V18-06

rejected.quote: Bar 6 was a failed trend line break in a steep bear trend, so it was a micro trend line low 1 short... Bar 10 was a strong up leg that broke the trend line...
rejected.reason: extended bar-by-bar figure narration (Figures 18.2-18.6) is discretionary chart commentary tied to specific historical charts, not a generalizable bar-level test; the recurring named patterns it references (low 1/low 2, micro trend line, moving average gap bar, spike and channel, wedge, expanding triangle, measured move) are primitives expected to be defined in other chapters of this book (e.g. counting/trend-line/climax chapters) and are not redefined here

chapter_summary: Argues that the first hour is dominated by patterns carried over from the prior session: gaps, breakouts of yesterday's channels/flags/trend lines, and the evaluation chain breakout -> failed breakout (reversal) -> failure of that failure (breakout pullback / resumption). Produces a generic opening-range-breakout rule, a moving-average gap proxy, the two-stage failed-breakout/breakout-pullback pair, a 'twice failed equals reversal' context filter, and a test-of-yesterday's-close reversal setup. Most of the chapter after the first two pages is one long bar-by-bar narration of five figures (18.1-18.6); that material was not mined candidate-by-candidate because it just re-applies named patterns (low 1/low 2, micro trend lines, spike-and-channel, measured moves, wedges, expanding triangles) that belong to other chapters, and the dedup pass should expect this chapter's contribution to be mostly the six candidates above.
